content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, the harlot (whore/prostitute) is a symbol of spiritual unfaithfulness to God — that is, idolatry and covenant apostasy pictured as marital infidelity. A people or religious system bound to God as a wife to a husband 'plays the harlot' by worshiping other gods, trusting foreign alliances, or embracing worldly/commercial corruption. This culminates in the figure of 'Babylon the Great, the mother of harlots' in Revelation 17, understood as a corrupt religious-political-economic system opposed to God, set in deliberate contrast to the faithful Bride of Christ.", "primary_basis": ["Hosea 1–3 (Hosea commanded to marry Gomer, a wife of whoredom, as a sign of Israel's unfaithfulness; e.g., Hosea 1:2; 2:2–13; 4:12–15)", "Ezekiel 16 (Jerusalem portrayed as an adulterous wife who played the harlot)", "Ezekiel 23 (Oholah and Oholibah — Samaria and Jerusalem as two harlot sisters)", "Jeremiah 2:20; 3:1–10 (Israel and Judah playing the harlot under every green tree)", "Isaiah 1:21 ('How the faithful city has become a harlot')", "Exodus 34:15–16; Leviticus 17:7; Deuteronomy 31:16; Judges 2:17 (idolatry described as 'whoring after other gods')", "Isaiah 23:15–17 and Nahum 3:4 (Tyre and Nineveh as harlots — commercial and political seduction of nations)", "Revelation 17:1–6, 15–18; 18:1–24; 19:2 (the great harlot Babylon, drunk with the blood of the saints)", "James 4:4 ('adulterous people, friendship with the world is enmity with God' — the underlying spiritual-adultery logic)", "Contrast passages: Ephesians 5:25–32; Revelation 19:7–8; 21:2, 9 (the faithful Bride, the counter-image to the harlot)"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "The harlot of Revelation 17 as imperial Rome — the idolatrous, persecuting, economically exploitative city/empire of John's day ('the city on seven hills'). This is the standard reading in critical and much mainstream scholarship.", "basis": ["Revelation 17:9 (seven mountains)", "Revelation 17:18 ('the great city that rules over the kings of the earth')", "1 Peter 5:13 ('Babylon' as code for Rome)"], "prominence": "dominant"}, {"meaning": "The harlot as an apostate or false end-times world religious system (often ecumenical/one-world religion) that rides and is later destroyed by the beast's empire — the dispensationalist/futurist reading.", "basis": ["Revelation 17:3–7, 16–17", "Revelation 13 (relationship to the beast)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "The harlot identified specifically with the papacy/Roman Catholic Church — the classic Protestant historicist reading of the Reformers (Luther, Calvin, the Westminster tradition, Seventh-day Adventism).", "basis": ["Revelation 17:4–6, 9, 18", "Revelation 18:4 ('Come out of her, my people')"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "The harlot as apostate Jerusalem/first-century Israel, judged in AD 70 — the preterist reading, drawing on the Old Testament pattern of Jerusalem as harlot.", "basis": ["Revelation 11:8 ('the great city... where their Lord was crucified')", "Ezekiel 16; 23; Isaiah 1:21 (Jerusalem-as-harlot precedent)", "Matthew 23:35–37 (blood of prophets on Jerusalem)"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "A distinct, positive usage: individual harlots (Rahab, Tamar, the woman of Luke 7) read as figures of faith, grace, Gentile inclusion, and redemption rather than as symbols of apostasy.", "basis": ["Joshua 2; 6:22–25", "Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25", "Matthew 1:5 (Rahab in Christ's genealogy)", "Matthew 21:31–32 ('tax collectors and prostitutes enter the kingdom before you')"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Purely literal readings — harlotry as sexual immorality only, or the Revelation harlot as a literal rebuilt city of Babylon — without broader symbolic covenant meaning.", "basis": ["Proverbs 5–7 (literal warnings, though many also read the adulteress as personified Folly opposite Lady Wisdom)", "Revelation 18 read hyper-literally of Babylon on the Euphrates"], "prominence": "rare"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "There is strong, long-standing consensus on the core symbolism: harlotry = covenant unfaithfulness/idolatry, the inverse of the marriage between God and his people (and Christ and the Church). This is uncontroversial across Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, and academic interpretation, rooted especially in Hosea, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. What is genuinely disputed is the specific referent of the great harlot in Revelation 17–18 (Rome, a future world religion, the papacy, or Jerusalem); these are alternative identifications within, not against, the shared symbolic meaning. The positive Rahab-type usage is a separate strand of usage rather than a competing symbolic definition."}
